stories.title: The Telescope in the Attic
paragraphs: Kenji had wanted a telescope for as long as he could remember. So when Aunt Ruth said she had an old one in her attic, he was up the ladder before she finished talking. The telescope was long and white, and it rested on three wobbly legs. A thick layer of dust covered everything, and one of the knobs was missing.

"It hasn't been used in twenty years," Aunt Ruth admitted. "It might need some work." Together they carried it down to the kitchen table. Kenji wiped away the dust with a soft cloth while his aunt searched a drawer for a knob that would fit. The best she could find was a wooden spool from her sewing basket. She glued it on and let it dry overnight.

The next evening, Kenji set up the telescope in the backyard. He pointed it at a bright, steady light that Aunt Ruth showed him and peered through the eyepiece. All he saw was a fuzzy gray blob. He turned the spool one way, then the other, until the blob shrank into a sharp, tiny circle. Beside the circle were four little dots in a row.

"That's Jupiter," Aunt Ruth said, leaning over his shoulder. "And those dots are some of its moons. A scientist named Galileo saw those same moons more than four hundred years ago." Kenji didn't want to blink. He stayed outside until his fingers were cold and his aunt had called him in three times.

For the rest of the week, clouds covered the sky every night. Kenji checked the window again and again. On Saturday, the clouds finally drifted away. Kenji grabbed a notebook and a pencil before he ran outside. This time he drew the moons, and he wrote the date at the top of the page. The next night, he drew them again. The dots had moved.

stories.title: Pepper Goes Missing
paragraphs: Every Friday, one student in Ms. Delgado's class got to take Pepper home for the weekend. Pepper was the class guinea pig, a round little animal with black and white fur. When it was finally Sofia's turn, she carried the cage home as carefully as if it held a birthday cake. Ms. Delgado had given her a list of rules. The most important one was underlined twice: Always latch the cage door.

On Saturday morning, Sofia cleaned the cage and gave Pepper fresh hay and a slice of cucumber. Then her little brother, Mateo, called her to come and see a funny cartoon. Sofia hurried to the living room and sat down next to him. Twenty minutes later, she came back to her bedroom and stopped in the doorway. The cage door was hanging open, and the cage was empty.

Sofia's heart thumped. She looked under the bed, behind the bookshelf, and inside her sneakers. There was no sign of Pepper anywhere. Mateo helped her search the hallway while Mom checked the kitchen. Sofia felt her eyes sting. How would she ever tell the class?

Then Sofia remembered something else from the list. Guinea pigs squeak when they hear a bag of food. She grabbed the crinkly bag of pellets and shook it hard. For a moment, the house was silent. Then a loud "Wheek! Wheek!" came from a pile of towels on the floor of the hall closet. Pepper was curled up in a warm nest between them.

Sofia laughed with relief and scooped her up. After that, she checked the latch every single time she closed the cage, and she even counted to three out loud while she did it. On Monday, she asked Ms. Delgado to add one more line to the list. It said, Never leave the room until the latch clicks.

stories.title: The Ball Over the Fence
paragraphs: Tariq had one rule about the yard next door: never go in. Mr. Halvorsen lived there, and he never smiled. He kept his grass cut short and his hedges perfectly square, and a sign on his gate said Please Keep Out. When Tariq practiced soccer against his garage wall, he aimed carefully so the ball would not fly over the fence.

One afternoon, Tariq tried a powerful new kick. The ball shot off his foot, sailed over the fence, and landed with a thud in Mr. Halvorsen's tomato bed. Tariq froze, and for a moment he considered leaving the ball there forever. Then he remembered that it was a birthday present from his grandmother. He took a deep breath, walked next door, and knocked.

Mr. Halvorsen opened the door with a frown. Tariq's words came out in a rush. "I'm sorry, my ball went in your garden, and I think it squashed a tomato plant, and I can help fix it." The old man looked at him for a long moment. Then he walked to the garden, picked up the ball, and spun it on one finger.

"That was a strong kick," he said. "But you lean back too far. That's why the ball goes so high." He set the ball on the grass and showed Tariq how to keep his body over the ball. When Tariq tried it, the ball flew low and straight, and Mr. Halvorsen nodded with approval. Then he pointed to an old photograph by his door. It showed a young man in a goalkeeper's shirt, diving through the air.

After that, Tariq visited every Saturday. He helped tie up the tomato plants, and Mr. Halvorsen helped with his kicks. Tariq still did not see him smile very often. But one day, Tariq noticed that the sign on the gate was gone.

stories.title: The Robot Race
paragraphs: For the school robot race, each team had to build a small robot that could follow a black line taped across the gym floor. Ingrid and Malik were partners. Ingrid loved writing code on the computer, and Malik loved building things with his hands. They spent two weeks after school putting their robot together. It had two wheels, a small battery, and a sensor underneath that could tell black from white. They named it Sprocket.

On the morning of the race, Sprocket rolled forward, wobbled, and drove straight off the line. Malik groaned. Ingrid stared at her code, but she could not find a single mistake. "It worked perfectly yesterday," she said. Their turn was in thirty minutes.

Malik got down on his knees and watched Sprocket carefully. He noticed that the robot always turned toward the left. He picked it up and spun each wheel with his finger. The right wheel turned smoothly, but the left one rubbed against a loose screw. "Found it!" he said. He tightened the screw while Ingrid held the robot still.

When their names were called, Sprocket rolled onto the starting line. This time it hummed along the tape, around both curves, and over the finish line. It was not the fastest robot in the gym. A team of fifth graders won first place, and Sprocket came in second.

Ingrid and Malik didn't mind. On the bus ride home, they were already sketching ideas for next year. Ingrid wanted to make the code faster around the curves. Malik wanted bigger wheels. "And this time," Ingrid said, "you check the screws, and I'll check the code."

stories.title: The Market Mistake
paragraphs: Every Saturday in summer, Mei helped her parents sell vegetables at the farmers market. Her job was the money box. She liked counting out change, and she was quick at adding numbers in her head. A bunch of carrots cost two dollars, a basket of peas cost three dollars, and a big bag of green beans cost four.

Late one morning, the market was so crowded that Mei could hardly keep up. A woman in a yellow hat bought peas and green beans and handed Mei a ten-dollar bill. Mei counted the change into her hand. Then the woman was gone, and the next customer was already waiting.

A few minutes later, Mei glanced at the money box and frowned. Something was not right. She added the numbers again in her head. Peas and green beans came to seven dollars, so the change should have been three dollars. But she had only handed the woman one.

Mei's stomach felt tight as she explained the problem to her dad, who looked at the long line of customers. "Can you find her?" he asked. Mei nodded. She took two dollar bills from the box and slipped through the crowd. She looked for the yellow hat at the honey stand, the bread stand, and the flower stand. At last she spotted it by the apple carts.

"Excuse me," Mei said, a little out of breath. "I made a mistake with your change. Here are the two dollars I owe you." The woman looked surprised at first, and then she smiled warmly. "I never would have noticed," she said. "Thank you for being so honest." The next Saturday, the woman in the yellow hat came to their stand first, and she brought two friends with her.

stories.title: The Solo
paragraphs: When Mr. Brooks announced that Adaeze would sing the solo at the spring concert, the whole choir clapped. Adaeze smiled, but her hands felt cold. She loved to sing in the shower, in the car, and while she walked the dog. Singing alone in front of three hundred people was a completely different thing.

Every evening for three weeks, she practiced the song in her bedroom. She sang it for her mother, for her little cousins, and even for the goldfish. Her mother gave her one piece of advice. "Pick one friendly face in the crowd," she said. "Then sing to that person as if no one else is there."

On the night of the concert, the gym was packed. Folding chairs filled the floor, and people stood along the back wall. When it was time for the solo, Adaeze stepped up to the microphone. Her knees were shaking. She took a breath and began the first line.

On the highest note, her voice cracked. It made a squeaky sound, like a door that needs oil. A few people in the front row giggled. For one terrible second, Adaeze wanted to run off the stage. Then she found her grandmother in the third row, smiling and nodding. Adaeze lifted her chin and kept singing.

When the song ended, the audience stood up and cheered. Afterward, Mr. Brooks shook her hand. "Anyone can sing a song when everything goes right," he said. "It takes a real performer to finish strong when something goes wrong." Adaeze thought about that all the way home. By the time she reached her front door, she had decided to try out for the solo again next year.

stories.title: The Map in the Book
paragraphs: Callum loved the used bookstore on Water Street because every book there had a history. One rainy afternoon, he bought a thick old book about trains for one dollar. When he opened it at home, a folded piece of paper slid out onto the floor. It was a hand-drawn map of his own town, but something about it looked strange.

Callum spread the map on the table. He recognized the river, the park, and Main Street. But a dotted line ran down the middle of Main Street, and little squares were drawn along it with labels like "Elm Stop" and "Mill Stop." At the top, someone had written "Trolley Line, 1912" in curly handwriting.

Callum had never seen a trolley in his town. He asked his dad, who shrugged and said, "Before my time." So on Saturday, Callum took the map to the town museum. A woman named Ms. Varga studied it with a magnifying glass. Her eyebrows went up. "Where did you find this?" she asked.

Ms. Varga explained that trolleys were like small trains that ran on rails in the street. Electric wires above the street gave them power. Long ago, people rode the trolley to work, to school, and to the lake. Later, when more families bought cars, the trolley stopped running, and the rails were covered by new roads. The museum had photographs of the trolley, but no one had ever found a map of every stop.

The museum asked if they could make a copy of Callum's map for a new display. A month later, Callum and his dad went to see it. The copy hung in a glass case next to a photo of a trolley full of smiling passengers. A small card under it said, "Found by Callum Reid." On the way home, Callum walked slowly down Main Street and tried to guess where Elm Stop had been.

stories.title: The Bake Sale Budget
paragraphs: The school library needed new beanbag chairs. Leila and her friends Theo and Jonah wanted to help, so they planned a bake sale. Their teacher gave them a budget of twenty dollars to buy supplies. Anything they earned after that would go to the library. Leila made a list right away. "Chocolate chip cookies," she said. "Everybody loves those."

At the store, the three friends added up what they needed. Chocolate chips, butter, flour, sugar, and eggs came to twenty-six dollars. That was six dollars over their budget. Theo wanted to buy fewer chocolate chips. Jonah wanted to skip the eggs. Leila said the cookies would fall apart without them.

Then Leila noticed a big sale sign by the bananas. Brown, spotty bananas were only ten cents each. Her grandmother baked banana muffins with bananas just like those. Leila called her and wrote the recipe on the back of her list. Banana muffins needed flour, sugar, eggs, butter, and bananas, but no chocolate chips at all. The new total was fifteen dollars.

Theo frowned. "Will people really buy muffins made from old bananas?" Leila grinned. "Spotty bananas are the sweetest ones," she said. With the five dollars they had left, the friends bought a small bag of chocolate chips anyway and sprinkled a few on top of each muffin.

On the day of the sale, the muffins were gone before lunch. The friends earned ninety dollars, which was enough for one beanbag chair. The librarian put a sign on it that said, "Thank you, Muffin Team!" Theo admitted that the spotty bananas had been a good idea after all.

stories.title: The Chess Surprise
paragraphs: Ravi had been playing chess for two years, and he almost always won. He played against his dad, his friends at chess club, and sometimes a computer program. So when his little sister, Anya, asked to play, Ravi laughed. "You don't even know how the knight moves," he said. Anya just set up the pieces and waited.

Ravi moved quickly, without thinking much, because he was certain the game would be over in ten minutes. But Anya studied the board for a long time before every move. She protected her queen carefully and moved her knights in their tricky L shapes. After twenty minutes, Ravi realized that he had lost two pawns and a bishop.

Ravi began to slow down. He leaned over the board and rested his chin in his hands. He tried a clever trap with his rook, but Anya saw it coming and moved her king out of the way. Then she slid her queen across the board. "Checkmate," she said quietly.

Ravi stared at the board, and his face felt hot. For a moment, he wanted to say that he had not really been trying. Then he looked at Anya. She was grinning, but she also looked a little nervous, as if she was waiting to see what he would say.

Ravi took a deep breath and held out his hand. "Good game," he said. "Where did you learn to play like that?" Anya pointed to the bookshelf. For the past three months, she had been reading his old chess books every night before bed. Ravi shook his head and laughed, and then he arranged the pieces again. "Best two out of three?" he asked.

stories.title: The Kite That Would Not Fly
paragraphs: Bao spent a whole Sunday building a kite. He used two thin sticks, a sheet of red paper, glue, and a long ball of string. On the front, he painted a dragon with gold eyes and a curling tail. When it was finished, he hung it on his bedroom wall and admired it all evening.

The next Saturday was breezy, so Bao and his dad carried the kite to the top of the hill in the park. Bao held the string, and his dad lifted the kite into the wind. It rose for a second, but then it spun around in circles and crashed nose first into the grass. They tried again and again. Each time, the kite spun and tumbled down.

Bao sat down on the grass and crossed his arms, ready to go home. His dad picked up the kite and turned it over. "I think it needs a real tail," he said. "A tail adds a little weight at the bottom. It keeps the kite pointing up into the wind, so it doesn't spin."

They didn't have any ribbon or string to spare. Bao looked around the hilltop, and then he pulled off the long striped scarf that his grandmother had knitted for him. His dad tied one end to the bottom of the kite. Bao held his breath as his dad tossed the kite into the air one more time.

This time, the kite climbed higher and higher. The dragon swayed back and forth, and the striped scarf waved below it. Other children on the hill stopped to watch in amazement. Bao let out more string until the kite was a small red speck against the clouds. That evening, he made a proper tail out of old ribbons. But he decided to keep the scarf with the kite, just in case.

stories.title: The Lunchroom Detectives
paragraphs: Zainab noticed it first. Every day after lunch, the big trash cans in the cafeteria were stuffed to the top. Half-eaten apples, banana peels, and crusts of bread spilled over the edges. "That's a lot of food going to waste," she said to her friend Eli. Eli shrugged. "It's just trash." But Zainab wasn't so sure.

She asked her teacher, Mrs. Abara, if their group could study the problem for a science project. For one week, Zainab, Eli, and two other classmates sorted the lunch trash while wearing rubber gloves. They put food scraps in one bucket, and they put paper, plastic, and everything else in another. Each afternoon, they weighed the buckets and wrote the numbers in a chart.

The results surprised everyone. More than half of the weight in the trash cans was food, and most of it was fruit and vegetable scraps. Zainab's grandfather kept a compost bin in his garden, where scraps rotted into rich, dark soil. If the school had compost bins, she thought, all those apple cores and peels could feed plants instead of filling up a landfill.

The group made a poster with their chart and gave a short talk to the principal. Eli explained the numbers, and Zainab explained how compost works. The principal asked a lot of questions. Then she said they could try two compost bins behind the school garden for one month.

At first, students kept throwing their scraps in the regular trash out of habit. So the group made bright green signs that said "Food Scraps Here!" and took turns standing by the bins at lunch. By the end of the month, the trash cans were only half full. The next spring, the school garden grew its biggest tomatoes ever. Eli admitted that it wasn't just trash after all.

stories.title: Tiny Tardigrades
paragraphs: If you collect a clump of damp moss and look at it under a microscope, you might spot a strange little creature. It has a round body, eight stubby legs, and tiny claws. It moves slowly, like a bear lumbering through the woods. Scientists call it a tardigrade, but many people call it a water bear.

Tardigrades are very small. Most are less than half a millimeter long, about the size of a grain of salt. Yet they live almost everywhere on Earth. They have been found on mountaintops, in deep oceans, in hot springs, and under thick ice. Many live right in backyard moss.

What makes tardigrades famous is how tough they are. When their home dries out, a tardigrade pulls in its legs and head and curls into a tiny dry ball called a tun. In this state, its body almost stops working. It does not eat, drink, or move. A tardigrade can stay this way for years. When water returns, it slowly uncurls and begins to crawl again.

Tardigrades in the tun state can survive things that would harm almost any other animal. They can live through freezing cold, and even great heat for a short time. In 2007, scientists even sent dried tardigrades into space on the outside of a spacecraft. When the tardigrades came back to Earth and got wet, some of them woke up and went on living.

Tardigrades are not superheroes, though. Most of the time, they need a thin film of water around them to stay active. Scientists hope that studying them could teach people new ways to protect things that dry out, such as medicines and seeds.

stories.title: Termite Towers
paragraphs: In the grasslands of Africa, some termites build towers of dirt that rise taller than a grown-up. From the outside, a termite mound looks like a lumpy pile of hard mud. Inside, it is full of tunnels and rooms. Millions of termites can live in a single colony.

Termites build their mounds one tiny bit at a time. Worker termites mix soil with their spit to make a kind of mud. They carry it in their mouths and press it into place. When the mud dries in the sun, it becomes almost as hard as brick. A tall mound can take years to build.

Most of the colony does not live in the tall tower. The queen, the workers, and the young termites live in a nest underground, below the mound. The tower above works like a giant chimney. Air moves through tunnels in its walls. It carries fresh air down toward the nest and lets stale air and extra heat escape.

Some of these termites are also farmers. They gather bits of dead grass and wood and carry them into special rooms in the nest. There, they grow a fungus that helps break down the plant material. The termites eat the fungus and the softened plants. The fungus needs steady warmth and damp air to grow, so the mound's moving air helps the farm too.

Engineers have studied termite mounds to learn how to cool buildings without using much electricity. A large office building in Zimbabwe was designed with ideas from termite mounds. Like a mound, it uses openings and chimneys to move air, so it stays comfortable inside even on hot days.

stories.title: Islands Made of Fire
paragraphs: The Hawaiian Islands sit in the middle of the Pacific Ocean. They are more than two thousand miles from the nearest continent. They did not break off from some larger piece of land. Every one of them was built by volcanoes, layer by layer, starting at the bottom of the sea.

Deep under this part of the ocean floor is a hot spot. It is a place where melted rock rises from far inside the Earth. The melted rock is called magma. When it pours out of the ocean floor, it is called lava. Each time lava cools, it hardens into a new layer of rock. After thousands of eruptions, the pile of rock can grow tall enough to rise above the waves. Then it is an island.

The hot spot stays in one place. But the ocean floor above it moves very slowly, a few inches each year. Over millions of years, each island is carried away from the hot spot, and its volcanoes stop erupting. Then a new volcano begins to grow over the hot spot. That is why the islands form a long chain.

Because of this, the islands are different ages. Kauai, in the northwest, is about five million years old. Its old volcanoes have worn down into steep green cliffs and deep valleys. The Big Island of Hawaii, in the southeast, is the youngest. It sits over the hot spot today, and its volcano Kilauea still erupts.

The next island has already started. About twenty miles off the coast of the Big Island, an underwater volcano is slowly growing. Its top is still more than three thousand feet below the waves. Scientists think it will not reach the air for tens of thousands of years, so no one alive today will ever stand on it.

stories.title: Emperor Penguin Dads
paragraphs: Emperor penguins are the largest penguins in the world. They live in Antarctica, the coldest place on Earth. Most animals leave before winter comes. Emperor penguins do something surprising instead. They raise their chicks during the long, dark winter. Fierce winds blow, and the temperature can drop far below zero.

In early winter, each female lays one egg. Then she does something that might seem strange. She carefully passes the egg to her mate and walks many miles back to the sea to hunt for fish. Making the egg used up much of her energy, and she needs to eat.

The father balances the egg on top of his feet. A warm fold of skin, called a brood pouch, covers it like a feathery blanket. For about two months, he stands in the cold and keeps the egg warm. He does not eat at all during that time. By the end, he may have lost almost half of his body weight.

To survive the bitter wind, thousands of fathers crowd together in a tight group called a huddle. The penguins in the middle stay warm, while the ones on the edges face the wind. The huddle moves slowly all the time. The birds on the outside shuffle in, and the birds in the middle drift out. In this way, every penguin gets a turn in the warm center.

Around the time the chick hatches, the mother returns with a belly full of fish. She finds her mate by listening for his special call among thousands of other penguins. She feeds the chick, and the hungry father finally heads to the sea to eat. From then on, the parents take turns caring for their chick until it is ready to swim on its own.
